newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura help to affiliate could pave way for others.
newsitem.headline: Nomura help to affiliate could pave way for others.

text.p: Nomura Securities Co Ltd's decision to provide financial aid to a troubled non-bank affiliate is seen in a positive light among industry analysts.
It could pave the way for other brokers to deal with similar loan problems at their units, they say.
"It was the right thing to do. It should be interpreted positively," said David Threadgold, a financial analyst at BZW Securities (Japan).

Shares in the top Japanese broker were down 30 yen (27 cents) to 1,950 yen ($17) at midday on Friday, after it announced late on Thursday it would provide support to the affiliate and post a special loss of 371 billion yen ($3.40 billion) in the half year to September 30.
Nomura vice president Atsushi Saito said the company would post a net loss for the first half as it did not plan to sell securities to help write off problem loans at the affiliate.
For the first five months, Nomura posted 59 billion yen ($541 million) in parent current profit, he said.

Several analysts said Nomura's net loss would total about 300 billion yen ($2.75 billion). Noting Nomura's profit in the first five months, James Fiorillo, an analyst at ING Baring Securities, said the firm was on track to record better than expected profits this year despite the market slump.

"Nomura seems to be following the lead of Japan's major banks, which reported massive losses last fiscal year in order to resolve the 'jusen' (mortgage firm) problem. We argue, as a result, that this is good news for the firm," Fiorillo said.
Analysts said not only Nomura but also other major brokers faced the prospect of having to deal with problem loans held by their non-bank affiliates.
BZW's Threadgold said he expects Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Daiwa Securities Co Ltd to make similar announcements for their non-bank affiliates.

Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd may face difficulty in helping to write off problem loans at its non-bank affiliates in the current business year, as it was undermined by a summer slump in the Tokyo stock market, analysts said. But Yamaichi will show its resolve to solve the group's problems as quickly as possible, they said.

Shares in Yamaichi ended the morning down 10 yen (9 cents) at 683 yen ($6). Nikko was steady at 1,170 yen ($10), and Daiwa was down 30 yen (27 cents) at 1,240 yen ($11). On Friday morning, the securities sector was the worst performing sector on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, down 1.26 percent compared with a 0.28 percent decline in the Nikkei average.

Market sources said the share price falls in second-tier brokerages followed downward earnings revisions by nine brokers on Thursday, of which seven said they would post parent current losses for the first half of 1996/97.
For the full year, however, almost all of the brokers expect profits.
Analysts said it would be difficult for many of them to meet their profit forecasts as their view of market activity for the second half was over-optimistic.
"Some of them must revise their forecast for 1996/97 again," one said. ($1=109 yen)
